Passionate Prayer
PASH-un-it prair
noun phrase (fervent, earnest prayer)
From “passionate” (Latin passio, suffering, strong feeling) and “prayer”; the fervent, wrestling, whole-hearted prayer that Scripture commends as effectual.

📖 Biblical Definition

Passionate prayer is the fervent, earnest, whole-hearted pleading with God that Scripture commends as effectual—not the babbling of vain repetition, but the wrestling of a soul that will not let go. James gives the charter: “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much,” and points to Elijah, a man of like passions, who prayed earnestly and shut and opened the heavens. The supreme pattern is the Lord Himself in Gethsemane, who, being in an agony, prayed more earnestly, His sweat as it were great drops of blood. Jacob wrestled until the breaking of the day and said, “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.” Epaphras labored fervently in prayer for the Colossians, that they might stand perfect and complete. The dictionary holds passionate prayer to be the ordinary temperature of a living faith: prayer that engages the whole man—mind, will, and affections—wrestling with God over sin, souls, and the advance of His kingdom. It marks the doctrine against two errors. The cold formalism that reduces prayer to a recited duty, drained of all fervor, is a denial of the very life of prayer; the dead heart prays no passionate prayer. But the opposite error must also be named: the charismatic and revivalist excess that mistakes emotional intensity, noise, or working oneself into a frenzy for true fervor. Biblical passion in prayer is not manufactured emotion but the earnestness of faith laying hold of God's promises; it may be loud as Hannah's silent moving lips were thought drunken, or quiet as a groan that cannot be uttered. The measure is not the volume but the faith, the importunity, and the conformity to God's will of the one who, like the Lord, prays “not my will, but thine, be done.”

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Fervent, earnest, whole-hearted prayer that Scripture commends as effectual (James 5:16); the wrestling of Jacob and the agony of Gethsemane—not cold formalism, nor manufactured emotional frenzy, but the earnestness of faith laying hold of God.

expand to see more

PASSIONATE PRAYER, noun phrase. Fervent, earnest, whole-hearted prayer that lays hold of God.

“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16).

Patterned by Christ in Gethsemane, who in agony prayed more earnestly (Luke 22:44).

By Jacob, who wrestled and would not let go without a blessing (Genesis 32:26).

Not cold formalism, nor manufactured frenzy, but the earnestness of faith.

📖 Key Scripture

Jas 5:16 — "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much."

Lu 22:44 — "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground."

Col 4:12 — "Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God."

Ge 32:26 — "And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Cold formalism drains prayer of all fervor, while charismatic-revivalist excess mistakes emotional intensity and worked-up frenzy for true fervor; both miss the earnestness of faith laying hold of God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is fervency grounded in faith. One corruption is the cold formalism that reduces prayer to a recited duty, drained of all earnestness—the lips moving while the heart is far away. Scripture rebukes it: the prayer that avails is fervent and effectual, the wrestling of a soul that will not let go. A faith that never prays passionately should examine whether it is alive at all, for the living soul cries out to God.

The opposite error, especially live in charismatic and revivalist circles, mistakes emotional intensity for spiritual fervor—measuring prayer by volume, working oneself into a frenzy, equating noise and feeling with faith. The dictionary distinguishes biblical passion from manufactured emotion. True fervency is the earnestness of faith laying hold of God's promises and submitting to His will, as the Lord in Gethsemane prayed in agony yet “not my will, but thine, be done.” It may be loud or silent—Hannah's lips moved without a sound and she was thought drunken—but its measure is the importunity and faith of the one praying, not the decibels. Passionate prayer wrestles with God like Jacob, and like Jacob bows to receive the blessing He gives.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin passio (strong feeling, suffering) and the prayer-words of Scripture: the Greek energoumene (“effectual, working”) and ektenos (“earnestly, fervently”).

expand to see more

Passio, Latin, strong feeling or suffering, the root of “passionate.”

Energoumene, Greek, “effectual” or “working,” of the prayer that avails (James 5:16).

Ektenesteron, Greek, “more earnestly,” of the Lord's prayer in agony (Luke 22:44).

Agonizomai, Greek, to strive or wrestle, of laboring fervently in prayer.

Jacob's wrestling (Genesis 32) is the Old Testament emblem of importunate prayer.

Usage

"The pastor called the cold congregation to passionate prayer, the fervent pleading that avails much."

"He warned the young zealots that biblical fervor is faith laying hold of God, not worked-up frenzy."

"She wrestled in prayer like Jacob, refusing to let go until the Lord should bless."
